939.title: Leo XIV (2025)
939.hook: Robert Prevost, an Augustinian from Chicago who served in Peru, becomes pope and greets the world with peace
939.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass, and after an election the new pope's name is added to those prayers in churches around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conclave: cards carried to the altar, ballots burned, a crowd watching a chimney. Your line was white smoke. What did you finally settle, and did it stay settled? Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

Peace be with you all. Those were the first words, spoken in Italian, by a new pope at the microphone on the balcony of Saint Peter's. They weren't about himself, or the vote, or the job. A cardinal had just announced him: Robert Francis Prevost, who had taken the name Leo. He grew up in Chicago. He spent years as a missionary in Peru. And he belongs to a religious order named for a bishop of North Africa, Augustine of Hippo. Today: the man on the balcony, and the four things he started with.
screen: `FIRST WORDS: PEACE BE WITH YOU ALL.` → `A NEW NAME: LEO.` → `CHICAGO, PERU, AUGUSTINE.`

segments.voice: First, those words. Leo said this greeting was the greeting of the risen Christ. He was pointing at a scene in John's Gospel. On the evening of the first Easter, the disciples are hiding behind shut doors, afraid, and Jesus comes and stands in the middle of them. In the Douay-Rheims his first words are simply: "Peace be to you." No blame for running away. Peace first. Second, the man. Robert Prevost joined the Order of Saint Augustine, friars who live in community under Augustine's rule. He went to Peru as a missionary, later served as bishop of Chiclayo, in the north of the country, and became a Peruvian citizen. On the balcony, after Italian, he switched to Spanish to greet his old diocese by name. Third, Augustine. In that first speech he quoted his order's founder, who once told his own congregation, in effect, that for his people he was a bishop, but with them he was a Christian. Augustine's point, as Leo used it: the man in white is first of all one more baptized person in the crowd. Fourth, the name. Speaking to the cardinals in the days after, Leo explained that he chose it partly for Leo the Thirteenth, the pope who wrote about the dignity and rights of workers when factories were remaking the world. Leo said the Church faces another such revolution now, in artificial intelligence, and wants to speak to it in the same spirit. So the new pope began with four things: a greeting from Easter evening, a missionary life, a line from Augustine, and a name chosen for a changing world.
screen: `PEACE: THE RISEN CHRIST'S GREETING.` · `CHICAGO, PERU, AND THE AUGUSTINIANS.` · `FOR THEM A BISHOP, WITH THEM A CHRISTIAN.` · `A NAME FOR A CHANGING WORLD.` · then, large: `PEACE BE TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a name the Church says at the altar. In the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass, the priest prays for the pope by name, and now that name is Leo. Settle, and breathe. Say the name once, slowly: Leo. Then think about what the job asks of one person: to speak for peace, to hold together a Church spread across the world, to get up tomorrow and do it again. If you pray, you can pray for him by name, in your own words or in silence. If you don't, hold him in mind the way you would anyone with a heavy job. Then let his first words come back to you: peace be with you all. The bell holds the time.
Leo the Fourteenth. Robert Prevost of Chicago, an Augustinian friar and a missionary bishop in Peru, elected pope, who greeted the world with peace.
Your line: peace be with you all. Today, greet one person with peace first, before you ask them for anything at all. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: Carlo Acutis (1991–2006)
940.hook: a teenager who built a website on Eucharistic miracles, now a canonized saint
940.howItsDone: Catholics visit Carlo Acutis's tomb in Assisi, keep his feast, and in some parishes show his exhibit on Eucharistic miracles; some young Catholics ask his prayers for their life online.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo the Fourteenth, a friar from Chicago by way of Peru. Your line was peace be with you all. Who did you greet with peace before asking for anything? Day nine hundred forty.

A teenager in Milan sits at the family computer, teaching himself to code. He isn't building a game. He's building a website. Country by country, he gathers accounts of Eucharistic miracles, stories of the bread and wine of the Mass tied to wonders, and lays them out as panels anyone could print and hang up. The same boy plays video games, makes silly films with his pets, and rations his own video games so they don't take over. His name was Carlo Acutis, and the Church now calls him a saint.
screen: `A TEENAGER TEACHES HIMSELF TO CODE.` → `A WEBSITE OF EUCHARISTIC MIRACLES.` → `NOW CALLED A SAINT.`

segments.voice: Carlo's story is short, so take it in four frames. First, the ordinary part. People who knew him remember a boy in jeans and sneakers, good with computers, who stuck up for classmates who were picked on and stopped to talk with homeless people near his home. Second, the website. He believed, as the Catholic Church teaches, that Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist, and he wanted people to notice. So he spent his spare time building an online exhibit of Eucharistic miracles, the way another kid might build a fan site. It has since been printed and shown in parishes far from Milan. Third, his line. Carlo used to say that the Eucharist was his highway to heaven, and those around him say he went to Mass whenever he could, every day if possible. The image was a teenager's own. The text behind it is older. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." As his family tells it, his days were built around that sentence. Fourth, his other remembered saying: that everyone is born an original, but many die as photocopies. He died young, of leukemia, offering his suffering, those with him said, for the pope and for the Church. He is buried in Assisi, where pilgrims file past his tomb. He was canonized together with Pier Giorgio Frassati, another young layman. Some Catholics point out what Carlo didn't do: he didn't flee the internet or drop his friends. He used the tools in front of him to point at what he loved.
screen: `AN ORDINARY BOY IN JEANS AND SNEAKERS.` · `A WEBSITE OF EUCHARISTIC MIRACLES.` · `THE EUCHARIST, MY HIGHWAY TO HEAVEN.` · `BORN ORIGINALS, NOT PHOTOCOPIES.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIVING BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: point your screen at something good, on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind your phone and the last few things you did on it. No guilt. Just notice. Then choose one small good thing to do with it after the bell: a kind message to someone who's struggling, a true and beautiful thing shared, a search for a food bank or a parish near you, or closing an app that drags you down. Hold that choice for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can offer your screen time to God the way Carlo offered his. If you don't, let the minute be quiet and unscrolled. The bell holds the time.
Carlo Acutis. A teenager from Milan who built a website on Eucharistic miracles, called the Eucharist his highway to heaven, and is now honored as a saint.
Your line: the eucharist, my highway. Today, do the one good thing you chose on your screen, and notice where your own highway is heading. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: The Jubilee of Hope (2025)
941.hook: a holy year of pilgrims of hope
941.howItsDone: In a jubilee year, Catholics make pilgrimages to Rome or to churches their bishop designates, pass through holy doors, go to confession and receive Communion, and pray for the pope's intentions to receive the jubilee indulgence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carlo Acutis, the teenager with the website. Your line was the eucharist, my highway. Where did you point your screen, and where did it take you? Day nine hundred forty-one.

A crowd moves slowly down the long avenue toward Saint Peter's. Parish groups in matching shirts. Families pushing strollers. An old man with a cane, keeping up. Some of them have come a very long way, and their shoes show it. Across the city, inside a Roman prison, another group is keeping the same holy year without leaving the building, because the pope came to them and opened a holy door there. Both groups are pilgrims. The year they are keeping has a name and a motto. The Jubilee of Hope. Pilgrims of hope.
screen: `A CROWD ON THE LONG AVENUE.` → `A HOLY DOOR IN A PRISON.` → `PILGRIMS OF HOPE.`

segments.voice: Jubilee starts in the book of Leviticus, where the Hebrew word is yovel. There God tells Israel to count off the years and then keep a special one: land goes back to the families who lost it, and people who had to sell themselves into service go free. In the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt sanctify the fiftieth year, and shalt proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land: for it is the year of jubilee." Remission means release, a debt let go. The Church borrowed that idea. Tradition holds that the first Catholic holy year was declared in the Middle Ages, and since then popes have proclaimed them from time to time, with pilgrims receiving an indulgence, the Church's word for a release from the punishment still due for sins already forgiven. Francis gave this jubilee its theme in a document called Spes non confundit, Latin for hope does not disappoint. The title is a line of Saint Paul to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "hope confoundeth not." Paul gives the reason straight after: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts. Then the pilgrim. A pilgrim isn't a tourist. A tourist goes to see something. A pilgrim goes in order to be changed on the way: the walking, the waiting, the sore feet, the prayer at the end. The jubilee asked Catholics to travel as pilgrims of hope, to Rome or to a church in their own diocese set aside for the year, and, in the old spirit of Leviticus, to let something go. Partway through the year, the pope who opened it died. A new pope carried it on. The pilgrims kept walking.
screen: `YOVEL: A YEAR OF RELEASE.` · `HOLY YEARS IN THE CHURCH.` · `HOPE DOES NOT DISAPPOINT.` · `A PILGRIM IS CHANGED ON THE WAY.` · then, large: `FOR IT IS THE YEAR OF JUBILEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a small pilgrimage. Settle, and breathe. A pilgrimage doesn't need a plane. Think of a place you could walk to that means something: a church, a cemetery, a park, a bench where someone you loved used to sit. Choose it now. Then picture the walk there, step by step, slowly, no headphones. Decide what you'll carry on the way, a hope or a worry, and what you'd like to set down when you arrive. If you pray, you can pray as you walk. If you don't, let the walking itself be the attention. The bell holds the time.
The Jubilee of Hope. A holy year opened by Francis, built on Paul's line that hope does not disappoint, with the motto pilgrims of hope.
Your line: pilgrims of hope. Today, make the small walk you chose, and when you arrive, set one thing down. Day nine hundred forty-one.

942.title: The world Church
942.hook: the Catholic Church's center of gravity shifts toward Latin America, Africa and Asia
942.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the same Mass in many languages and musical styles, and some parishes in Europe and North America are served by priests and religious sisters from Africa, Asia and Latin America.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jubilee of Hope: pilgrims on the long avenue to Saint Peter's, and a holy door opened inside a prison. Your line was pilgrims of hope. What did you set down when you arrived? Day nine hundred forty-two.

Some Sunday mornings now look like this. In a small town in the American Midwest, the priest at the altar grew up in Nigeria. In a parish in Ireland, the homily comes in the accent of southern India. In Kinshasa, a choir comes up the aisle dancing, with drums. In Manila, the doors are open because the crowd won't fit inside. And in Rome, the last two popes came from Buenos Aires and from a missionary life in Peru. Same Mass, same prayers, many languages. Today is about where the Catholic Church lives now.
screen: `A NIGERIAN PRIEST IN THE MIDWEST.` → `DRUMS IN KINSHASA.` → `POPES FROM THE AMERICAS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. The Creed at Mass calls the Church catholic, and the Catechism says plainly what that means: universal. A church for everyone, everywhere. For long stretches of history, though, the center of Catholic life sat in Europe: its bishops, its universities, the missionaries it sent out. That picture has changed. Writers who follow the Church describe its center of gravity moving south, toward Latin America, Africa and Asia, and they point to the Church's own yearly statistics to show it. You can see it at a great Mass in Rome now, in the languages of the readings and in the faces of the newest cardinals. Catholics read their oldest texts as pointing this way from the start. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." And at Pentecost, in Acts, the crowd in Jerusalem is Jews gathered from far and wide, "devout men, out of every nation under heaven," each hearing the apostles speak in his own language. Some readers call Pentecost the Church's birthday, and notice that on its first day it already spoke more than one language. The shift isn't a tidy story. In some places the faith arrived with missionaries who traveled alongside colonial powers, and that history includes real harm, which the Church has had to face. But the faith also spread through local catechists, mothers and grandmothers, and converts who made it their own and sang it to their own music. Today the traffic runs in every direction: African and Asian priests serve European parishes, Latin American theologians are read in seminaries far away, and bishops from every continent sit together at synods in Rome. The church moved south. It also kept moving.
screen: `CATHOLIC: UNIVERSAL.` · `A CENTER OF GRAVITY MOVING SOUTH.` · `EVERY NATION UNDER HEAVEN.` · `TRAFFIC IN EVERY DIRECTION.` · then, large: `GOING THEREFORE, TEACH YE ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the Church in Africa. Settle, and breathe. Africa is a whole continent, not one place, so let one face or one city come to mind: a priest you've met, a choir you've heard, a country you know only by its name on a map. Hold it there. Now picture a parish somewhere on that continent getting ready for Sunday. Someone sweeping the floor. Someone tuning a drum. A catechist walking in from a village. If you pray, you can pray for that parish and its people. If you don't, simply wish them well, by name if you have one. The bell holds the time.
The world Church. The Catholic Church as it is now: on every continent, with its center of gravity moving toward Latin America, Africa and Asia.
Your line: the church moved south. Today, learn one thing about the Catholic Church in a country you've never visited: a saint, a song, a bishop, a feast. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
943.hook: an Eastern Catholic church outlawed under Soviet rule that survived underground
943.howItsDone: Ukrainian Greek Catholics celebrate the Byzantine Divine Liturgy in Ukrainian and other languages, in Ukraine and in parishes abroad, and honor the bishops, priests and laypeople who were imprisoned or killed under Soviet rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world Church: on every continent, its center of gravity moving. Your line was the church moved south. What did you learn about the Church somewhere you've never been? Today, a church that had to go under the ground. Day nine hundred forty-three.

A small apartment in Soviet Ukraine, late at night, the curtains drawn. A man who spends his days as a laborer takes a folded cloth from a drawer, spreads it on the kitchen table, and sets out bread and a cup. A few neighbors have come in quietly, one at a time, so no one notices a crowd. He is a priest, and this is the Divine Liturgy, sung almost in a whisper. Accounts from those years describe scenes like this. Officially, his church does not exist. Today is the church that kept existing anyway.
screen: `CURTAINS DRAWN, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A KITCHEN TABLE FOR AN ALTAR.` → `A CHURCH THAT DOESN'T EXIST.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church worships the way Orthodox Christians in Ukraine do: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, married men among its parish priests. And it is in full communion with the pope. Greek in its name means the Byzantine tradition, not the country. It is one of the Eastern Catholic churches, which keep their own rites and their own laws while belonging to the one Catholic Church. Second, the ban. After the Second World War, Soviet authorities set out to erase it. Its bishops were arrested. A gathering held under state pressure declared the church dissolved and its parishes joined to the Russian Orthodox Church. Priests who refused were sent to labor camps. Its head, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj, spent years in the camps before he was released to Rome. Third, the underground. The church didn't vanish. It went into kitchens, forests and cemeteries. Bishops were ordained in secret. Priests held ordinary jobs and served at night. Grandmothers baptized babies quietly and taught the prayers at home. Catholics read those years through a promise in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." A kitchen table was enough. Fourth, the return. As Soviet rule loosened toward its end, the church came out of hiding, and its people filled their churches openly again. It's a story with wounds on more than one side: Orthodox believers suffered under the same regime, and churches in Ukraine still carry that history together. But the underground church kept the Liturgy going in the dark until it could sing it in daylight.
screen: `EASTERN WORSHIP, IN COMMUNION WITH ROME.` · `DECLARED DISSOLVED BY THE STATE.` · `KITCHENS, FORESTS AND CEMETERIES.` · `OUT OF HIDING, INTO DAYLIGHT.` · then, large: `THERE AM I IN THE MIDST OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe with both lungs. John Paul the Second liked to say the Church has to breathe with both its lungs, East and West. Settle, and take a slow breath, and notice it fill both sides of your chest. Keep breathing that way. With each breath, let one of the Eastern Catholic churches come to mind, even if all you know is a name: Ukrainian, Melkite, Maronite, Syro-Malabar, and others, some of them living through war or exile right now. If you pray, you can pray for them on each breath. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath each. The bell holds the time.
The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. An Eastern Catholic church of the Byzantine tradition, in communion with Rome, outlawed under Soviet rule, that survived underground.

944.title: Catholics under pressure today
944.hook: in some countries Christians practice their faith at real risk
944.howItsDone: Catholics pray for persecuted Christians in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, some parishes light their churches red on a day of remembrance, and charities support communities under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the underground church: a Liturgy at a kitchen table, until it could be sung in daylight. Your line was the underground church. Whose quiet faithfulness did you notice? Day nine hundred forty-four.

Open an old calendar of martyrs and the scenes come easily: arenas, emperors, ancient Rome. Then open the news. In Nicaragua, a Catholic bishop, Rolando Álvarez, is sentenced to prison and later sent out of the country. In Nigeria, a parish in the town of Owo is attacked during Mass on Pentecost Sunday. In other places, believers meet quietly, because meeting openly could cost them a job, their freedom, or more. Yesterday's underground church is a story with an ending. Today's stories are still going on.
screen: `AN OLD CALENDAR OF MARTYRS.` → `A BISHOP IN PRISON, THEN EXILE.` → `A PARISH ATTACKED AT MASS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word the Church uses for those killed for the faith: martyr. The Church keeps their names, and it is still adding to them. The Acts of the Apostles tells of one of the earliest: Stephen, one of seven men the community chose to serve at its tables, stoned for what he preached. As the stones fall, he prays for the men throwing them, asking the Lord not to hold this sin against them. Second, the Gospel never promised otherwise. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Pressure isn't treated as a sign that something went wrong. It's named ahead of time. Third, remembering. The letter to the Hebrews asks its readers to remember prisoners as if they were in chains alongside them, and to remember those who suffer as people living in the same kind of body. That is one reason Catholics in a quiet suburb pray for a parish in Nigeria or a bishop far from home: in that letter's picture, they are not strangers in a headline. Fourth, what pressure looks like now. Sometimes it is violence. Often, those who track it say, it is quieter: laws that close schools and charities, a job lost after a baptism, a priest followed by police, a church that can never get a building permit. And it isn't only Christians. Believers of other faiths face it too, in other places, and the Second Vatican Council taught that religious freedom belongs to every person. Some parishes light their buildings red on a chosen day, red for the martyrs. Others read names aloud at Mass. The point is the same as the old calendars: the names are said, so they are not forgotten.
screen: `STEPHEN PRAYS FOR HIS KILLERS.` · `PERSECUTION, NAMED AHEAD OF TIME.` · `AS IF IN CHAINS WITH THEM.` · `QUIETER PRESSURE, AND NAMES SAID ALOUD.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one community under pressure. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where believers practice at risk, from the news or from today's lesson. If you know a name, use it. If you don't, think of one parish, one family, getting dressed for Sunday knowing what it might cost them. Stay with them for a few slow breaths. In the same sermon, Jesus asks his listeners to pray for those who persecute them, too. If you pray, you can pray for both. If you don't, hold them all in mind with respect. The bell holds the time.
Catholics under pressure today. Believers in our own time who practice their faith at real risk, the Church's newest witnesses.
Your line: not only long ago. Today, look up one Christian community under pressure right now, and say its name or its town out loud once. Day nine hundred forty-four.

945.title: New movements
945.hook: lay movements like Focolare and Sant'Egidio work for unity and peace
945.howItsDone: Catholics join lay movements and associations such as Focolare, Sant'Egidio and the Saint Vincent de Paul Society, meeting for prayer and Scripture and serving the poor, usually alongside their parish life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholics under pressure today: a bishop sent into exile, a parish attacked at Mass, names said aloud. Your line was not only long ago. Whose name or town did you say? Day nine hundred forty-five.

Trent, in northern Italy, during the Second World War. The bombs are falling, and a young schoolteacher named Chiara Lubich crowds into an air-raid shelter with a few friends. They've brought one book, the Gospels, and they read it by candlelight, asking what would still stand if everything else fell. They keep landing on Jesus's prayer that his followers may all be one. Years later, in Rome, a group of high school students starts meeting to read the Gospel and then going out to the poor on the edge of the city. Neither group was started by a bishop or a priest. Today is what grew out of rooms like those.
screen: `A BOMB SHELTER IN TRENT.` → `ONE BOOK BY CANDLELIGHT.` → `STUDENTS IN ROME.`

segments.voice: First, Focolare. Chiara's circle became the Focolare movement. Focolare is Italian for hearth, the fire a family gathers around, and that was the idea: small communities living the Gospel together like a family at the fire. Their key text is Jesus's prayer at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Focolare took it to heart, building friendships with other Christians, with people of other faiths, and with people of none. Second, Sant'Egidio. The Roman students, gathered by Andrea Riccardi, took their name from a small church in the Trastevere neighborhood. Their life rests on three things: prayer each evening, friendship with the poor, and peace. That last one reached all the way to a war: talks held at their house in Rome helped bring the civil war in Mozambique to an end. Third, who leads. These movements are led by laypeople, people who aren't priests or vowed religious, with jobs and families. The Second Vatican Council taught that the laity share in the Church's mission by their own calling, through baptism, not as helpers on loan from the clergy. Movements like these are one shape that teaching took. Priests and bishops belong to some of them, but the founders were a teacher and a student. Fourth, the week. Look back over it: a pope greeting the world with peace, a teenager with a website, pilgrims walking, a church on every continent, a church underground, believers under pressure. And now laypeople leading. One Church, seen through different doors.
screen: `FOCOLARE: A HEARTH.` · `SANT'EGIDIO: PRAYER, THE POOR, PEACE.` · `THE LAITY SHARE THE MISSION.` · `ONE CHURCH THROUGH DIFFERENT DOORS.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a lay movement near you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the place where you live. Somewhere near it there may be laypeople already at work: a parish group running a food pantry, a prayer circle in someone's living room, a Saint Vincent de Paul group collecting coats, a Focolare or Sant'Egidio community, a Catholic Worker house. Let one come to mind, or decide what you'd look for. Choose one to look up after the bell. Then rest your hands in your lap and notice what they could carry for an hour a week. If you pray, you can ask where they're needed. If you don't, let the question sit quietly. The bell holds the time.
New movements. Communities like Focolare and Sant'Egidio, started and led by laypeople, working for unity, for the poor and for peace.
Your line: laypeople lead. Today, look up the one group you chose and find out when it next meets. Day nine hundred forty-five.
